AC-1.o: Write down how access to your systems is decided and controlled, and the steps people follow to do it. Everything else in this family rests on this.
AC-1.a: Write an access control policy (who may access what, who approves, how often it is reviewed) and a procedure for granting, changing and removing access. Name an owner, publish both, and review them on a set schedule and after major changes.
AC-1.e: An assessor asks for the approved policy and procedure, checks they are current and reviewed on schedule, and asks staff whether they know them.
AC-1.r: Approved access control policy; access procedure; review history; distribution or acknowledgement records.
AC-1.s: Develop, document, and disseminate to [organisation-defined]: [organisation-defined] access control policy that: Addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance; Is consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines; Procedures to facilitate the implementation of the access control policy and the associated access controls; Designate an [organisation-defined] to manage the development,…

AC-2.o: Manage every account on the system from request to removal: who has one, why, what it can do, and when it goes away.
AC-2.a: Define which account types are allowed, name account managers, require approval before an account is created, record each account's role and access, review accounts regularly, and disable accounts promptly when people leave or change jobs.
AC-2.e: An assessor samples accounts and traces each to an approved request, checks recent leavers were disabled on time, and looks for evidence of periodic account reviews.
AC-2.r: Account request and approval records; list of accounts with owners and roles; account review records; leaver and mover tickets.
AC-2.s: Define and document the types of accounts allowed and specifically prohibited for use within the system; Assign account managers; Require [organisation-defined] for group and role membership; Specify: Authorized users of the system; Group and role membership; Access authorizations (i.e., privileges) and [organisation-defined] for each account; Require approvals by [organisation-defined] for requests to create accounts; Create, enable, modify, disable, and remove accounts in accordance with [organisation-defined]; Monitor the use of accounts; Notify account…

AC-2(1).o: Use tools, not manual steps, to help create, change, review and remove accounts, so fewer mistakes slip through.
AC-2(1).a: Use a directory or identity management system (for example Active Directory or an identity platform) to manage accounts, feed it from HR where possible, and use its reports for reviews.
AC-2(1).e: An assessor checks which tool manages accounts and sees it in use for creation, change and removal.
AC-2(1).r: Identity system configuration; HR feed or workflow description; automated account reports.
AC-2(1).s: Support the management of system accounts using [organisation-defined].

AC-2(2).o: Temporary and emergency accounts must switch themselves off after a set time, so they cannot be forgotten and left open.
AC-2(2).a: Decide how long temporary and emergency accounts may live, then configure the system to disable or remove them automatically when that time runs out.
AC-2(2).e: An assessor looks at the setting and checks that past temporary or emergency accounts were removed on time.
AC-2(2).r: Expiry settings; list of temporary and emergency accounts with creation and removal dates.
AC-2(2).s: Automatically [organisation-defined] temporary and emergency accounts after [organisation-defined].

AC-2(3).o: Switch off accounts that should no longer work: expired, unowned, misused, or unused for too long.
AC-2(3).a: Set a time limit for disabling such accounts and a maximum inactivity period, then configure or run a regular job that disables accounts meeting those conditions.
AC-2(3).e: An assessor looks for inactive or orphaned accounts that are still enabled and checks the inactivity setting.
AC-2(3).r: Inactivity and expiry settings; disabled-account reports; review records.
AC-2(3).s: Disable accounts within [organisation-defined] when the accounts: Have expired; Are no longer associated with a user or individual; Are in violation of organizational policy; or Have been inactive for [organisation-defined].

AC-2(4).o: Every time an account is created, changed, enabled, disabled or removed, the system records it automatically.
AC-2(4).a: Turn on logging of account management events in your directory and systems, and send the logs where they are kept and reviewed.
AC-2(4).e: An assessor makes or finds an account change and checks it appears in the logs with who did it and when.
AC-2(4).r: Audit log settings; sample log entries for account changes.
AC-2(4).s: Automatically audit account creation, modification, enabling, disabling, and removal actions.

AC-2(5).o: People must sign out when they are expected to, for example at the end of a shift or after a set idle time.
AC-2(5).a: Decide when users must log out, tell them, and back it up with technical settings such as automatic sign-out after inactivity.
AC-2(5).e: An assessor checks the written rule and the matching session or sign-out settings.
AC-2(5).r: Log-out rule in policy or rules of behaviour; session timeout settings.
AC-2(5).s: Require that users log out when [organisation-defined].

AC-2(6).o: Privileges can change on the fly while someone is working, based on rules, rather than being fixed until an administrator steps in.
AC-2(6).a: Decide which privileges may change dynamically and under what conditions, then implement it with the access management tooling and test it.
AC-2(6).e: An assessor asks for the rules and sees privileges being granted and withdrawn as those rules say.
AC-2(6).r: Dynamic privilege rules; tool configuration; test results.

AC-2(7).o: Administrator and other powerful accounts are handled with extra care: set up deliberately, watched, and removed when no longer needed.
AC-2(7).a: Keep privileged accounts separate from everyday ones, grant them through a defined role scheme, monitor role changes, and remove privileges promptly when a person's duties change.
AC-2(7).e: An assessor lists privileged accounts, checks each is justified and monitored, and looks for timely removal after role changes.
AC-2(7).r: Privileged account list and approvals; role definitions; monitoring alerts; removal records.
AC-2(7).s: Establish and administer privileged user accounts in accordance with [organisation-defined]; Monitor privileged role or attribute assignments; Monitor changes to roles or attributes; Revoke access when privileged role or attribute assignments are no longer appropriate.

AC-2(8).o: Accounts are created and removed automatically as they are needed, for example for short-lived services or devices.
AC-2(8).a: Identify which accounts are dynamic, and configure the system to create, activate and deactivate them automatically with appropriate controls.
AC-2(8).e: An assessor checks which accounts are created dynamically and how their lifecycle is controlled.
AC-2(8).r: Dynamic account design; configuration; lifecycle logs.
AC-2(8).s: Create, activate, manage, and deactivate [organisation-defined] dynamically.

AC-2(9).o: Shared and group accounts hide who actually did something, so they are only allowed under strict conditions.
AC-2(9).a: Decide the conditions under which a shared account is acceptable (for example, only with a named custodian and password change when someone leaves), and remove any that do not meet them.
AC-2(9).e: An assessor lists shared accounts and checks each meets the stated conditions.
AC-2(9).r: Shared account register with justification and custodian; conditions in policy.
AC-2(9).s: Only permit the use of shared and group accounts that meet [organisation-defined].

AC-2(11).o: Accounts may only be used under set conditions, such as certain times, places or devices.
AC-2(11).a: Decide the usage conditions for each account type (for example office hours or managed devices only) and enforce them with system settings.
AC-2(11).e: An assessor checks the conditions are written down and enforced by the system.
AC-2(11).r: Usage conditions; access policy or conditional access settings.

AC-2(12).o: Watch accounts for unusual behaviour, such as sign-ins at odd hours or from odd places, and report it.
AC-2(12).a: Define what counts as atypical use, set up monitoring or alerts for it, and route alerts to named people who act on them.
AC-2(12).e: An assessor looks at the monitoring rules and at alerts that were raised and followed up.
AC-2(12).r: Atypical usage criteria; alert rules; alert and follow-up records.
AC-2(12).s: Monitor system accounts for [organisation-defined]; Report atypical usage of system accounts to [organisation-defined].

AC-2(13).o: When someone becomes a high risk, for example facing dismissal or suspected of wrongdoing, their accounts are disabled quickly.
AC-2(13).a: Agree with HR and security what makes someone high risk and how fast their accounts must be disabled, and set up the process so it happens within that time.
AC-2(13).e: An assessor checks the process and asks for examples where it was followed on time.
AC-2(13).r: High-risk disablement procedure; HR notifications; disablement timestamps.
AC-2(13).s: Disable accounts of individuals within [organisation-defined] of discovery of [organisation-defined].

AC-3.o: The system must actually enforce who may see or change what. Approved access on paper is not enough.
AC-3.a: Configure permissions in systems and applications to match approved access, deny by default, and test that people cannot reach what they have not been granted.
AC-3.e: An assessor tries or reviews access for sample users and checks it matches what was approved.
AC-3.r: Access control configuration; permission reports; test results.
AC-3.s: Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.

AC-3(2).o: Some sensitive actions need two people to approve, so no single person can do them alone.
AC-3(2).a: Decide which actions need dual authorisation (for example deleting backups or releasing funds) and configure the system to require a second approver.
AC-3(2).e: An assessor checks the list of dual-authorisation actions and sees the system require two people.
AC-3(2).r: List of dual-authorisation actions; configuration; approval logs.

AC-3(3).o: Access is decided by the system based on labels such as classification, and users cannot change or pass it on themselves.
AC-3(3).a: Where required, use a platform that enforces mandatory access control, define the labels and rules, and apply them consistently across the system.
AC-3(3).e: An assessor checks that labels and rules exist and that users cannot override them.
AC-3(3).r: Mandatory access control policy; labelling scheme; system configuration.
AC-3(3).s: Enforce [organisation-defined] over the set of covered subjects and objects specified in the policy, and where the policy: Is uniformly enforced across the covered subjects and objects within the system; Specifies that a subject that has been granted access to information is constrained from doing any of the following; Passing the information to unauthorized subjects or objects; Granting its privileges to other subjects; Changing one or more security attributes (specified by the policy) on subjects, objects,…

AC-3(4).o: Owners of information decide who else may access it, within the limits the organisation sets.
AC-3(4).a: Define what owners may and may not share, configure the system so owners can grant access within those limits, and review what owners have shared.
AC-3(4).e: An assessor checks the rules and samples owner-granted access against them.
AC-3(4).r: Discretionary access policy; permission reports; review records.
AC-3(4).s: Enforce [organisation-defined] over the set of covered subjects and objects specified in the policy, and where the policy specifies that a subject that has been granted access to information can do one or more of the following: Pass the information to any other subjects or objects; Grant its privileges to other subjects; Change security attributes on subjects, objects, the system, or the system’s components; Choose the security attributes to be associated with newly created or revised objects; or Change the…

AC-3(5).o: Security-critical information, such as keys and security settings, can only be reached when the system is in a safe maintenance state.
AC-3(5).a: Identify the security-relevant information, and restrict access to it to controlled maintenance or secure states.
AC-3(5).e: An assessor checks what is protected and how access outside secure states is prevented.
AC-3(5).r: List of security-relevant information; access restrictions; configuration.
AC-3(5).s: Prevent access to [organisation-defined] except during secure, non-operable system states.

AC-3(7).o: Grant access through roles, such as 'payroll clerk', rather than person by person.
AC-3(7).a: Define roles and the permissions each needs, assign people to roles, and manage access by changing role membership.
AC-3(7).e: An assessor checks role definitions and that users' access comes from their roles.
AC-3(7).r: Role catalogue with permissions; role assignments; review records.
AC-3(7).s: Enforce a role-based access control policy over defined subjects and objects and control access based upon [organisation-defined].

AC-3(8).o: When someone's attributes change, such as clearance or job, the access that depended on them is taken away.
AC-3(8).a: Link access to the attributes it depends on and set rules for revoking access, including how fast, when those attributes change.
AC-3(8).e: An assessor checks the revocation rules and examples of access removed after a change.
AC-3(8).r: Revocation rules; change and revocation records.
AC-3(8).s: Enforce the revocation of access authorizations resulting from changes to the security attributes of subjects and objects based on [organisation-defined].

AC-3(9).o: Information only leaves the system when the receiver can protect it and the release has been checked.
AC-3(9).a: Define which receivers are allowed and what protection they must provide, and check information before it is released outside the system.
AC-3(9).e: An assessor checks the release rules and evidence that releases followed them.
AC-3(9).r: Release rules; receiver agreements; release logs.
AC-3(9).s: Release information outside of the system only if: The receiving [organisation-defined] provides [organisation-defined]; [organisation-defined] are used to validate the appropriateness of the information designated for release.

AC-3(10).o: In an emergency, automatic access controls can be overridden, but only by named people, and every override is recorded.
AC-3(10).a: Define when override is allowed and by whom, set up the override so it is logged, and review each use.
AC-3(10).e: An assessor checks the override conditions and the logs of any overrides.
AC-3(10).r: Override procedure; authorised roles; override logs and reviews.
AC-3(10).s: Employ an audited override of automated access control mechanisms under [organisation-defined] by [organisation-defined].

AC-3(11).o: Places holding especially sensitive types of information get tighter access than the rest of the system.
AC-3(11).a: Identify those information types and where they are stored, and restrict access to those stores to people who need it.
AC-3(11).e: An assessor checks the list of sensitive repositories and who can access them.
AC-3(11).r: Sensitive repository list; access lists; review records.
AC-3(11).s: Restrict access to data repositories containing [organisation-defined].

AC-3(12).o: Applications must declare what access they need when installed, and cannot quietly take more later.
AC-3(12).a: Require applications to declare their access needs, enforce those limits (for example mobile or platform permissions), and approve any later changes.
AC-3(12).e: An assessor checks how application permissions are declared, enforced and approved.
AC-3(12).r: Application permission policy; platform settings; approval records.
AC-3(12).s: Require applications to assert, as part of the installation process, the access needed to the following system applications and functions: [organisation-defined]; Provide an enforcement mechanism to prevent unauthorized access; Approve access changes after initial installation of the application.

AC-3(13).o: Access is decided by attributes, such as department, location or device, rather than fixed lists.
AC-3(13).a: Define the attributes and rules that decide access, and implement them in an attribute-based access control system.
AC-3(13).e: An assessor checks the rules and tests that access follows them.
AC-3(13).r: Attribute and policy definitions; system configuration; test results.
AC-3(13).s: Enforce attribute-based access control policy over defined subjects and objects and control access based upon [organisation-defined].

AC-3(14).o: People can get access to the personal information you hold about them.
AC-3(14).a: Provide a way (a portal, form or process) for individuals to see the personal information you hold about them, and verify who they are first.
AC-3(14).e: An assessor checks the mechanism exists, works, and verifies identity.
AC-3(14).r: Individual access procedure; request log; response records.
AC-3(14).s: Provide [organisation-defined] to enable individuals to have access to the following elements of their personally identifiable information: [organisation-defined].

AC-3(15).o: Use both owner-controlled and system-controlled access rules together where the policy calls for it.
AC-3(15).a: Define which information falls under each kind of rule, and configure the system to enforce both.
AC-3(15).e: An assessor checks both kinds of rule are defined and enforced.
AC-3(15).r: Access control policy; configuration for both models.
AC-3(15).s: Enforce [organisation-defined] over the set of covered subjects and objects specified in the policy; Enforce [organisation-defined] over the set of covered subjects and objects specified in the policy.

AC-4.o: Control where information is allowed to go, inside the system and to connected systems, not just who can read it.
AC-4.a: Define which flows are allowed between networks, systems and zones, and enforce them with firewalls, gateways, proxies or data loss prevention.
AC-4.e: An assessor compares the allowed-flow rules with firewall and gateway configurations.
AC-4.r: Information flow policy; network diagram; firewall and gateway rule sets.
AC-4.s: Enforce approved authorizations for controlling the flow of information within the system and between connected systems based on [organisation-defined].

AC-4(1).o: Flow decisions use labels attached to the information, such as its classification.
AC-4(1).a: Attach security or privacy attributes to information and configure flow controls to act on them.
AC-4(1).e: An assessor checks the attributes used and the rules that act on them.
AC-4(1).s: Use [organisation-defined] associated with [organisation-defined] to enforce [organisation-defined] as a basis for flow control decisions.

AC-4(2).o: Separate, protected processing areas are used to keep flows apart.
AC-4(2).a: Use protected domains (for example separate virtual environments or enclaves) to enforce flow control between types of information.
AC-4(2).e: An assessor checks how domains are separated and how flows between them are controlled.
AC-4(2).s: Use protected processing domains to enforce [organisation-defined] as a basis for flow control decisions.

AC-4(3).o: Flow rules can change quickly in response to conditions, such as an attack or a change in mission.
AC-4(3).a: Define the conditions and the flow rule changes they trigger, and implement the ability to apply them dynamically.
AC-4(3).e: An assessor checks the dynamic rules and how they are triggered.
AC-4(3).r: Dynamic flow rules; triggering conditions; change logs.

AC-4(4).o: Encrypted traffic must not be allowed to slip past inspection just because it is encrypted.
AC-4(4).a: Decide how encrypted traffic is handled (decrypt and inspect, block, or allow only from approved endpoints) and configure your gateways accordingly.
AC-4(4).e: An assessor checks the approach and the gateway settings that enforce it.
AC-4(4).r: Encrypted traffic policy; inspection or blocking configuration.
AC-4(4).s: Prevent encrypted information from bypassing [organisation-defined] by [organisation-defined].

AC-4(5).o: Limit hiding one kind of data inside another, such as files embedded in documents, which can smuggle content past controls.
AC-4(5).a: Set limits on embedded data types and enforce them with content filtering.
AC-4(5).e: An assessor checks the limits and the filters that enforce them.
AC-4(5).r: Embedded data rules; content filter configuration.
AC-4(5).s: Enforce [organisation-defined] on embedding data types within other data types.

AC-4(6).o: Flow decisions take the information's metadata, such as author or classification, into account.
AC-4(6).a: Decide which metadata matters and configure flow controls to use it.
AC-4(6).e: An assessor checks which metadata is used and how.
AC-4(6).s: Enforce information flow control based on [organisation-defined].

AC-4(7).o: Some flows must be one way only, enforced by hardware such as a data diode.
AC-4(7).a: Identify where one-way flow is needed and install hardware that physically allows traffic in one direction.
AC-4(7).e: An assessor checks where one-way devices are used and that they are in place.
AC-4(7).r: Architecture showing one-way devices; device specifications.
AC-4(7).s: Enforce one-way information flows through hardware-based flow control mechanisms.

AC-4(8).o: Filters check information against security and privacy rules before it moves, and decide what happens when a filter fails.
AC-4(8).a: Define the filters, where they apply, and what happens to data if filtering fails (for example block it), and configure them.
AC-4(8).e: An assessor checks filter rules and the behaviour on failure.
AC-4(8).r: Filter definitions; failure handling rules; configuration.
AC-4(8).s: Enforce information flow control using [organisation-defined] as a basis for flow control decisions for [organisation-defined]; [organisation-defined] data after a filter processing failure in accordance with [organisation-defined].

AC-4(9).o: Some transfers need a human to review them before they go.
AC-4(9).a: Define which flows need human review and under what conditions, and put a review step in the process.
AC-4(9).e: An assessor checks the conditions and records of reviews carried out.
AC-4(9).s: Enforce the use of human reviews for [organisation-defined] under the following conditions: [organisation-defined].

AC-4(10).o: Privileged administrators can switch security or privacy filters on and off, but only in defined conditions.
AC-4(10).a: Define when filters may be disabled and by whom, restrict the capability to those administrators, and log its use.
AC-4(10).e: An assessor checks the conditions and logs of filters being enabled or disabled.
AC-4(10).r: Filter control procedure; admin roles; change logs.
AC-4(10).s: Provide the capability for privileged administrators to enable and disable [organisation-defined] under the following conditions: [organisation-defined].

AC-4(11).o: Privileged administrators can configure filters to support different policies.
AC-4(11).a: Give authorised administrators the ability to configure filters, and control and record changes.
AC-4(11).e: An assessor checks who can configure filters and how changes are controlled.
AC-4(11).s: Provide the capability for privileged administrators to configure [organisation-defined] to support different security or privacy policies.

AC-4(12).o: When data moves between security domains, its type is checked to support the flow decision.
AC-4(12).a: Use data type identifiers (such as file signatures) to validate data before it crosses domains.
AC-4(12).e: An assessor checks how data types are identified and validated at the boundary.
AC-4(12).s: When transferring information between different security domains, use [organisation-defined] to validate data essential for information flow decisions.

AC-4(13).o: Complex data is broken into parts so each part can be checked against policy when crossing domains.
AC-4(13).a: Configure cross-domain solutions to decompose information into checkable parts before filtering.
AC-4(13).e: An assessor checks the decomposition approach in the cross-domain solution.
AC-4(13).s: When transferring information between different security domains, decompose information into [organisation-defined] for submission to policy enforcement mechanisms.

AC-4(14).o: Only data in fully defined, expected formats may cross between domains.
AC-4(14).a: Define allowed formats and structures, and configure filters to reject anything else.
AC-4(14).e: An assessor checks the allowed formats and that others are rejected.
AC-4(14).r: Format specifications; filter configuration; rejection logs.
AC-4(14).s: When transferring information between different security domains, implement [organisation-defined] requiring fully enumerated formats that restrict data structure and content.

AC-4(15).o: Information crossing domains is checked for content that should not be there, and blocked if found.
AC-4(15).a: Define what counts as unsanctioned information (for example malware or restricted keywords), scan for it, and block transfers that contain it.
AC-4(15).e: An assessor checks the scanning rules and records of blocked transfers.
AC-4(15).r: Unsanctioned content definitions; scanning configuration; block logs.
AC-4(15).s: When transferring information between different security domains, examine the information for the presence of [organisation-defined] and prohibit the transfer of such information in accordance with the [organisation-defined].

AC-4(17).o: Both ends of a transfer are identified and authenticated before information flows.
AC-4(17).a: Authenticate source and destination points (for example with certificates or device identity) for information transfers.
AC-4(17).e: An assessor checks how endpoints are authenticated.
AC-4(17).s: Uniquely identify and authenticate source and destination points by [organisation-defined] for information transfer.

AC-4(19).o: Metadata is checked as carefully as the data itself when crossing domains.
AC-4(19).a: Apply the same filtering and validation to metadata as to content at domain boundaries.
AC-4(19).e: An assessor checks that metadata is validated.
AC-4(19).s: When transferring information between different security domains, implement [organisation-defined] on metadata.

AC-4(20).o: Only approved solutions are used to move sensitive information across domains.
AC-4(20).a: Use cross-domain solutions that are approved for the purpose, and do not allow ad hoc transfer methods.
AC-4(20).e: An assessor checks the solutions in use are approved ones.
AC-4(20).s: Employ [organisation-defined] to control the flow of [organisation-defined] across security domains.

AC-4(21).o: Different kinds of information flow are kept apart, physically or logically.
AC-4(21).a: Separate flows (for example with VLANs, separate networks or encryption) according to the type of information and required protection.
AC-4(21).e: An assessor checks how flows are separated.
AC-4(21).s: Separate information flows logically or physically using [organisation-defined] to accomplish [organisation-defined].

AC-4(22).o: One device can reach several security domains without letting information pass between them.
AC-4(22).a: Use solutions that give access to multiple domains from one device while blocking flow between them.
AC-4(22).e: An assessor checks the solution prevents cross-domain flow.
AC-4(22).r: Multi-domain access solution design; test results.
AC-4(22).s: Provide access from a single device to computing platforms, applications, or data residing in multiple different security domains, while preventing information flow between the different security domains.

AC-4(23).o: Information that must not be released is modified or removed before transfer.
AC-4(23).a: Define how non-releasable information is handled (redacted, removed or replaced) and apply it at the boundary.
AC-4(23).e: An assessor checks the modification rules and sample transfers.
AC-4(23).s: When transferring information between different security domains, modify non-releasable information by implementing [organisation-defined].

AC-4(24).o: Incoming data is taken apart and rebuilt in a clean standard form, which strips out hidden or malformed content.
AC-4(24).a: Configure cross-domain solutions to parse incoming data into a normalised format and regenerate it.
AC-4(24).e: An assessor checks the normalisation step.
AC-4(24).s: When transferring information between different security domains, parse incoming data into an internal normalized format and regenerate the data to be consistent with its intended specification.

AC-4(25).o: Data is cleaned before it crosses domains, to remove things that could leak information or carry attacks.
AC-4(25).a: Define what must be sanitised and how, and apply it at the boundary.
AC-4(25).e: An assessor checks sanitisation rules and their application.
AC-4(25).s: When transferring information between different security domains, sanitize data to minimize [organisation-defined] in accordance with [organisation-defined].

AC-4(26).o: What the filters did, and what they found, is recorded.
AC-4(26).a: Log content filtering actions and results at domain boundaries and keep the logs for review.
AC-4(26).e: An assessor checks filtering is logged.
AC-4(26).s: When transferring information between different security domains, record and audit content filtering actions and results for the information being filtered.

AC-4(27).o: More than one independent filter checks each data type, so one failing filter does not let bad data through.
AC-4(27).a: Use redundant, independent filtering mechanisms for each data type.
AC-4(27).e: An assessor checks for independent redundant filters.
AC-4(27).s: When transferring information between different security domains, implement content filtering solutions that provide redundant and independent filtering mechanisms for each data type.

AC-4(28).o: Filters run in a fixed sequence that cannot be skipped.
AC-4(28).a: Build a linear filter pipeline enforced by access controls so data must pass every stage.
AC-4(28).e: An assessor checks the pipeline cannot be bypassed.
AC-4(28).s: When transferring information between different security domains, implement a linear content filter pipeline that is enforced with discretionary and mandatory access controls.

AC-4(29).o: An orchestration engine makes sure every filter runs, in the right order, without errors.
AC-4(29).a: Use a filter orchestration engine that checks completion, order and results of each filtering step.
AC-4(29).e: An assessor checks the orchestration engine's checks.
AC-4(29).s: When transferring information between different security domains, employ content filter orchestration engines to ensure that: Content filtering mechanisms successfully complete execution without errors; Content filtering actions occur in the correct order and comply with [organisation-defined].

AC-4(30).o: Filtering is split across several processes so one compromised process does not undo it all.
AC-4(30).a: Implement content filtering with multiple processes.
AC-4(30).e: An assessor checks the filtering design uses multiple processes.
AC-4(30).s: When transferring information between different security domains, implement content filtering mechanisms using multiple processes.

AC-4(31).o: Content that failed filtering never reaches the receiving domain.
AC-4(31).a: Configure transfer solutions to stop failed content being delivered.
AC-4(31).e: An assessor checks failed content is blocked.
AC-4(31).s: When transferring information between different security domains, prevent the transfer of failed content to the receiving domain.

AC-4(32).o: The process moving data between filter pipelines only moves it; it does not filter, and it checks the filtering really happened.
AC-4(32).a: Design the transfer process to validate filtering metadata and move only content that passed all filtering.
AC-4(32).e: An assessor checks the transfer process design.

SA-11(4).o: Developers review critical code by hand.
SA-11(4).a: Require manual code review of defined code using defined methods.
SA-11(4).s: Require the developer of the system, system component, or system service to perform a manual code review of [organisation-defined] using the following processes, procedures, and/or techniques: [organisation-defined].

SA-15(11).o: Developers archive what they release with the evidence from the final security review.

SA-15(13).o: Developers use a consistent, structured logging format that makes logs useful for security analysis.

SA-17(6).o: Security-relevant parts are structured to be testable.
SA-17(6).s: Require the developer of the system, system component, or system service to structure security-relevant hardware, software, and firmware to facilitate testing.

SA-17(9).s: Use different designs for [organisation-defined] to satisfy a common set of requirements or to provide equivalent functionality.

SA-21.o: Developers of defined systems are screened and cleared.

SA-22.o: Replace components that are no longer supported by the maker, or arrange alternative support.

SC-1.o: Write down how systems and their communications are protected.

SC-1.s: Develop, document, and disseminate to [organisation-defined]: [organisation-defined] system and communications protection policy that: Addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, management commitment, coordination among organizational entities, and compliance; Is consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines; Procedures to facilitate the implementation of the system and communications protection policy and the associated system and communications…

SC-2.o: Keep admin functions separate from what ordinary users use.
SC-2.a: Separate management interfaces from user interfaces (for example separate admin consoles, networks or servers).
SC-2.e: An assessor checks management and user functions are separated.
SC-2.s: Separate user functionality, including user interface services, from system management functionality.

SC-2(1).o: Ordinary users never see admin functions in their interfaces.
SC-2(1).a: Hide management functionality from non-privileged users.
SC-2(1).s: Prevent the presentation of system management functionality at interfaces to non-privileged users.

SC-2(2).o: Store application state separately to help protect privacy.
SC-2(2).a: Store state information from applications and software separately.
SC-2(2).s: Store state information from applications and software separately.

SC-3.o: Isolate security functions from everything else so they cannot be tampered with.
SC-3.a: Isolate security functions using separate domains, processes or hardware.
SC-3.s: Isolate security functions from nonsecurity functions.

SC-3(1).o: Use hardware separation to isolate security functions.
SC-3(1).s: Employ hardware separation mechanisms to implement security function isolation.

SC-3(2).o: Isolate access and flow control functions from other functions.
SC-3(2).s: Isolate security functions enforcing access and information flow control from nonsecurity functions and from other security functions.

SC-3(3).o: Keep non-security functions out of the security boundary.
SC-3(3).e: An assessor checks the boundary contents.
SC-3(3).s: Minimize the number of nonsecurity functions included within the isolation boundary containing security functions.

SC-3(4).o: Build security functions as independent, well-contained modules.
SC-3(4).a: Implement modules with high cohesion and low coupling.
SC-3(4).s: Implement security functions as largely independent modules that maximize internal cohesiveness within modules and minimize coupling between modules.

SC-3(5).o: Build security functions in layers where lower layers do not depend on higher ones.
SC-3(5).s: Implement security functions as a layered structure minimizing interactions between layers of the design and avoiding any dependence by lower layers on the functionality or correctness of higher layers.

SC-4.o: Stop information leaking between users through shared resources, such as memory or disk.
SC-4.a: Clear shared resources before reuse and prevent unintended transfer.
SC-4.e: An assessor checks resource clearing mechanisms.
SC-4.s: Prevent unauthorized and unintended information transfer via shared system resources.

SC-4(2).o: When a system switches between classification levels, clear shared resources first.
SC-4(2).a: Apply defined procedures when switching levels.
SC-4(2).s: Prevent unauthorized information transfer via shared resources in accordance with [organisation-defined] when system processing explicitly switches between different information classification levels or security categories.

SC-5.o: Protect against or limit the effects of denial-of-service attacks.

SC-5(1).s: Restrict the ability of individuals to launch the following denial-of-service attacks against other systems: [organisation-defined].

SC-5(2).o: Manage capacity and redundancy to absorb flooding attacks.
SC-5(2).s: Manage capacity, bandwidth, or other redundancy to limit the effects of information flooding denial-of-service attacks.

SC-5(3).o: Monitor for signs of denial-of-service attacks and resource exhaustion.
SC-5(3).a: Use defined monitoring tools and watch defined resources.
SC-5(3).s: Employ the following monitoring tools to detect indicators of denial-of-service attacks against, or launched from, the system: [organisation-defined]; Monitor the following system resources to determine if sufficient resources exist to prevent effective denial-of-service attacks: [organisation-defined].

SC-6.s: Protect the availability of resources by allocating [organisation-defined] by [organisation-defined].

SC-7(3).s: Limit the number of external network connections to the system.

SC-7(4).e: An assessor checks interfaces and reviews.
SC-7(4).s: Implement a managed interface for each external telecommunication service; Establish a traffic flow policy for each managed interface; Protect the confidentiality and integrity of the information being transmitted across each interface; Document each exception to the traffic flow policy with a supporting mission or business need and duration of that need; Review exceptions to the traffic flow policy [organisation-defined] and remove exceptions that are no longer supported by an explicit mission or business…

SC-7(5).o: Block all traffic by default and allow only what is needed.
SC-7(5).a: Configure firewalls to deny by default and allow by exception.

SC-7(5).s: Deny network communications traffic by default and allow network communications traffic by exception [organisation-defined].

SC-7(9).s: Detect and deny outgoing communications traffic posing a threat to external systems; Audit the identity of internal users associated with denied communications.

SC-7(10).o: Prevent data being smuggled out, and test that prevention.
SC-7(10).a: Implement exfiltration prevention (for example DLP) and test it at a set frequency.
SC-7(10).e: An assessor checks controls and test results.
SC-7(10).s: Prevent the exfiltration of information; Conduct exfiltration tests [organisation-defined].

SC-7(11).s: Only allow incoming communications from [organisation-defined] to be routed to [organisation-defined].

SC-7(14).s: Protect against unauthorized physical connections at [organisation-defined].

SC-7(15).s: Route networked, privileged accesses through a dedicated, managed interface for purposes of access control and auditing.

SC-7(17).a: Use protocol validation (for example application-layer gateways).
